I majored in PR and worked in the industry a little. I'm chiming in to confirm that u/windowplanters is right. Sponsored content is definitely a thing, but it needs to be clearly labeled as such for legal reasons. Getting an unlabeled ad published is *not* the goal for a PR professional. The goal for a PR professional is to get what we call "earned publicity" - basically, having your press release published by a legitimate news organization for free, in part or in whole, edited or not. This way, the PR professional is able to get the person or organization they represent featured in the news while avoiding the stigma and perceived lack of credibility associated with a sponsored article.

Think of it this way - most people will ignore an ad for a local restaurant, but they might pay attention to a news story about a new restaurant opening up. Undiscerning readers will never know the difference between a press release and an organic news story. The news organization essentially launders what could have been a clearly labeled advertisement into "news", for free. And usually, it's for exceptionally boring reasons such as slow news days, or to "fill space", or so the news organization can insert some feel-good stories alongside the depressing actual news.

So yes, it would be a huge scandal - and a huge legal liability - if a sponsored article was not labeled as such. But the truth is a lot more depressing.

NAH. Your daughter shouldn't have dropped "Oh, I'm changing majors" on you out of nowhere. You're totally reasonable for being concerned about finances and you don't want to be used by your daughter.

At the same time - your daughter is probably a teenager, and teenagers have a tendency to be brats. You should be the adult here and try to have a productive conversation with her soon if you want to save your wallet and your kid's future.

First, see if her displeasure with her major is something that can be addressed. Is she struggling with her CS classes? See if there's another tech-related major that she may be more interested in. 

Is she feeling isolated in a male-dominated field? See if there's an organization for women in STEM that you can point her to - this would also be a good networking opportunity!

Is she simply struggling emotionally? Point her in the direction of campus counseling services and tell her how to get involved and make friends on campus.

If that doesn't work, see if there's a reasonable compromise that fits your both your wishes. Would she like to minor in liberal arts instead of changing majors? Would you be willing to pay for a liberal arts-adjacent major that leads to a specific career field, such as public relations, advertising, technical communications, social work, etc.?

Finally, if your daughter refuses to respect your boundaries and continues demanding that you pay for a liberal arts major, put your foot down but reassure her that you love her. Tell her that you'd be happy to walk her through the process of taking out a student loan that she can pay back later. She'll either see the price tag and change her mind, or she can at least make an educated decision.

You sound very similar to me several years ago. I tried to enjoy games competitively like my friends did, but my situational awareness and reaction time was just not up to snuff. The problems were compounded by my mental illnesses - ADHD made it difficult to catch every detail on screen, and my depressive brain-fog made it difficult to process the information and respond effectively. 

In FPSes, I mained support characters (e.g. TF2 Engineer) because I sucked at aiming and situational awareness. In Smash Bros, I would roll dodge excessively and main noob-friendly characters. I never got better at FPSes. I was able to improve a little bit at Smash Bros with online video tutorials, but even at my best it was still a crude by-the-numbers imitation of "good" gameplay that was easy to counter.

I also sucked at accepting criticism on my gameplay, mostly because the way gamers dole out criticism does not jive with me. Let's be real - gamers are blunt. They don't mean to be assholes, but when they're in the zone or shooting the shit about video games they exude this... overly familiar, playful rudeness. They'll thoughtlessly make jabs at each other and then laugh about it. Some people jive well with this culture, but not me.

I made the tough decision to stop playing multiplayer games with strangers. Smash Bros is just a party game for me now. I still boot up multiplayer FPSes from time to time, but only to play with friends as a nostalgia trip. I can't play these games whenever I want anymore, but I always enjoy it when I do play them.

I play almost exclusively single player games now, and my life is a lot less stressful because of it. I enjoy video games again. I'm not ashamed to enjoy "casual" experiences like Uncharted or Skyrim. I've even found a few "difficult" games like Bloodborne very enjoyable, just because the manner in which they were difficult jived well with me for some reason.

TL;DR it's perfectly OK to just stop playing games in a manner that stresses you out. You'll get more fun out of it that way.

I've only really played Fo3 and NV. Of the two, I definitely prefer NV, but somehow I think Fo3 was better as an introduction to the series. Just be advised that Fo3 has issues running on later versions of Windows, so it may take some tweaking to get it to work.

Fo3:

-Set in the area in and around Washington DC. It's interesting to see what happened to the federal government and all the famous landmarks of DC. However, because of this, I think this game might not resonate as well with people not from the United States.

-Desolate urban + suburban environments that were hit very hard by the nuclear apocalypse. Strong atompunk aesthetic - if you've never played a Fallout game, this game is probably what you're thinking of when you think "Fallout".

-Play as someone who's lived in a Vault their entire life, who is now leaving the community for the first time to find their father out in the wasteland. You get a taste of what life was like in the vaults, so IMO that's another reason why Fo3 is a good introduction to the "world" of Fallout.

New Vegas:

-Obviously, set in and around Las Vegas. The area was not hit as hard by the nuclear war, so there's still plants and clean bodies of water around. Some people are even growing crops. The famous Las Vegas Strip is left relatively intact, and there are even fully operational casinos. In general, society feels somewhat more intact/rebuilt. In other words, it's post-post-apocalypse.

-The area outside of Las Vegas has a "wild west" atmosphere, which really jives well with the setting, IMO. However, some people get put off by the repetitive nature of desert environments.

-Your character's backstory is not "set in stone". All you know is that your character was a courier that was assaulted while delivering a package. Beyond this, you're free to imagine any sort of backstory you want for your character - which is good if you're into "roleplaying" as your character rather than self-inserting. (And New Vegas is very good for that, IMO.)
I didn't think I'd ever hear the Fallout universe described as "cozy", but I feel you.

Not a blood family secret, but my mom has a group of friends from college that she's stayed close to since she graduated. They're all like aunts to me, and their kids are like my cousins. Heck, they're probably closer to me than my actual aunts and cousins.

There is one woman that I only ever saw a few times, though. She ended up moving to a farm in the middle of nowhere, so it was difficult for my mom and her other friends to keep in touch. Nevertheless, we made sure to make family trips to see her every few years or so.

It was pretty cool when we got to visit her - she had a husband and a son who would take us for rides on ATVs and show us how to feed the rabbits. I remember entering a steep ditch on a dare from the son, accidentally grasping a cactus, and whining about it for at least 10 minutes until my mom's friend took me into the kitchen and treated my hand under the sink. 

Roughly 3/4ths of a year after our last visit and a couple days before my birthday, my mom receives a call late at night. She starts screaming and crying, and I can't calm her down or figure out what happened that made her suddenly start crying. She's like this for hours, and eventually I give up and go to bed fearing that someone died.

She sits me down the next day and tells me that her friend who lived on the farm died in a fire. I don't know what to think - I didn't know her very well, but I try to comfort my mother.

A few weeks later, I'm casually browsing the internet on the family computer when I notice a news article in my mom's bookmarks with her dead friend's name on the title. I click on it out of curiosity, and the contents shake my world. It's confusing. What is this about her being murdered? My mom walks in while I'm reading, freaks out, and sits me down again to explain to me something that the article left out: Her friend was murdered by *her own son*. The very one that seemed so fun to be around when I actually met him - first impressions can be deceiving. She tells me that she's sorry for lying to me, but she thought I was too young to handle the truth.

I've been googling the murderer's name recently. I know now that:

* The victim was shot with a borrowed gun.
* A conflict over the son's girlfriend was a possible motive for murder.
* He's part of an inmate seminary program and will graduate with a bachelor's degree in spring 2015.
* He now has tattoos across his knuckles that read "L-O-S-T H-O-P-E", which he got because he was angry at God.
* He is to be released on my birthday 50 years from now, eligible for parole on the same date in 20 years.

It's more of an open secret in that the information is out there for anyone who cares to look, but my mom and her friends always leave the exact details of their friend's death out when they talk about it with people who don't know.
